claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has an FCC matrix.
The AM process produces inherent microsegregation in this alloy.
Elevated-temperature oxidizing or reducing gases selectively oxidize or reduce primarily Al and Ti at surfaces and grain boundaries.
Selective reaction forms a brittle, non-adherent oxide or reduced-phase scale.
Spallation of the surface scale triggers local elemental segregation and cracking.
Scale spallation, segregation, and cracking precipitate catastrophic failure.
The proposed structural mediator is a continuous, brittle, Al/Ti-rich oxide or reduced-phase layer coupled to segregation at grain boundaries and surface regions.
Under oxidizing conditions, preferential oxidation of Al and Ti forms a brittle oxide scale.
Thermal cycling and inherent stresses cause the oxide scale to crack and spall.
Scale spallation exposes fresh alloy, accelerates segregation at critical boundaries, and nucleates internal cracks.
Reducing conditions suppress oxide-scale formation and thereby improve specimen integrity.
Changing the gas environment or applying an oxidation-resistant coating will inhibit the proposed surface reaction.
Oxidizing exposure or absence of a coating will produce a thicker, continuous, brittle scale.
Oxidizing exposure or absence of a coating will produce greater segregation and higher crack density.
The greater scale formation, segregation, and cracking under oxidizing exposure will reduce mechanical integrity.
Reducing or inert atmospheres, or an oxidation-inhibiting coating, will reduce scale formation and segregation and delay or prevent catastrophic failure.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily at approximately 600 degrees Celsius or above and after exposure long enough for scale formation and microstructural degradation.
At lower temperatures or very short exposure times, reaction and segregation kinetics are too slow to cause extensive degradation.
Unmodified specimens exposed to either oxidizing or reducing gases form oxide or reduced phases and subsequently fail mechanically.
A lack of statistically significant environmental or coating effects on scale formation, segregation, cracking, and mechanical integrity would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis says reducing gases can selectively reduce reactive elements and form a brittle reduced-phase scale that contributes to failure, whereas the mechanism states that reducing conditions diminish the degradation pathways and improve integrity.

The baseline groups reducing-gas exposure with oxidizing exposure as producing unmitigated phase formation and mechanical failure, while the mechanism and prediction treat reducing exposure as protective.
